new_statements.translation: 2000 fn. 5: 'It is difficult for us to be precise about the problem of accent in Zenaga. The observations made for Berber seem generally valid for this dialect, notably its light character and its lack of distinctive function (Chaker 1995: 98). As for the place of the accent, however, we are tempted to adopt for Zenaga, not the Kabyle rule opposing nouns and verbs, but the one formulated by J. Lanfry for Ghadames (1968: 325), which opposes accent on the 1st syllable for the imperative and aorist (éknəf, yéknəf) to accent on the 2nd syllable for the preterite (iknéf).'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (1) Taine-Cheikh 2020, 'Zenaga', Oxford Handbook of African Languages 530-542, HAL author ms; HAL cover page confirms the citation). extracted text per page: heading '2.3 Syllable structure' is on pdf p.4, and pdf p.5 lines 3-5 read exactly: 'Lexemes in general consist of two or three syllables, sometimes they are monosyllabic and often they consist of more than three syllables (in particular inflected verbs). Stress is rarely marked and is not fixed. It is important as phrasal accent and moves towards the end of the word if clitic(s) is/are present.' -- verbatim as quoted, immediately before '3 Morphology'. (2) Cohen & Taine-Cheikh 2000, BSL 95(1); HAL cover says pp. 269-322…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the principal describer, Zenaga word stress is weak (rarely perceptible), non-contrastive and has no fixed position; prominence functions mainly as a phrasal accent, shifting toward the end of the word when clitics attach. Tentative partial observations: in verbs, accent on the 1st syllable in imperative/aorist vs 2nd syllable in the preterite (2000, hedged 'nous sommes tentes'); accent 'seems to depend exclusively on syllable structure' (2008, Berber in Contact p. ~118); the author states (2025 fn. 2) that no exhaustive study of Zenaga accentuation exists.
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics pull the accent toward the end of the word (2020); genitive connector n is never accented and each noun of a genitive phrase tends to keep its own accent (2025); vowel length is independent of accent (2023 EB; 2000).
new_statements.domain_note: Author explicitly frames prominence as chiefly phrasal ('important as phrasal accent'); word+clitic group is the accentual unit; statements are impressionistic, not instrumental (the 1997 acoustic study measured vowels only).
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Zenaga of south-west Mauritania (Trarza), Taine-Cheikh's data chiefly from an Idab Lahsen (Idābləḥsan) speaker (M. Ould Ahmedou Yahya); same language as zena1248, no separate dialect glottocode needed.

new_statements.translation: It is difficult for us to be precise about the problem of accent in Zenaga. The observations made for Berber seem valid in general for this dialect, notably its light character and its lack of distinctive function (S. Chaker, 1995: 98). Concerning the place of the accent, however, we are tempted to adopt for Zenaga not the accentuation rule opposing nouns and verbs as in Kabyle (Chaker, idem: 98-9) but the one formulated by J. Lanfry for Ghadames (1968: 325), which opposes accentuation on the 1st syllable for the imperative and the aorist (éknәf, yéknәf) to accentuation on the 2nd syllable for the preterite (iknéf).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog rule for Zenaga is empty and the existing statement (Taine-Cheikh 2020, sect. 2.3: stress rarely marked, not fixed, phrasal) is read as unclear. This 2000 paper is compatible with 'not fixed' and adds detail: accent is light and non-distinctive, and its position is tentatively aspect-conditioned (initial in imperative/aorist, second syllable in preterite, after Lanfry's Ghadames rule), with accent shift under suffixation. It gives no fixed-position rule, so the catalog's blank rule stands; the tentative alternation is worth recording as a note, not as a rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The authors say they cannot be precise about Zenaga accent. Accent is light and has no distinctive (contrastive) function. As a tentative placement rule they borrow Lanfry's Ghadames rule: first syllable in the imperative and aorist, second syllable in the preterite, i.e. an aspect-conditioned alternation rather than a fixed position. In the body text (ms. p. 5) they also note that certain suffixations shift the accent and reduce the preceding short vowels (e.g. yuˀṃœš 'it became ground' + plural -œn > ʊˀṃœššœn), and that long vowels are not restricted to accented position, though accented long vowels are longer than the others.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the whole placement rule is offered only tentatively ('nous sommes tentés de reprendre'), and the shift of accent under suffixation is noted without a rule
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Zenaga of Mauritania (data of the Idab Lahsen region, Taine-Cheikh's field data), the same variety as the catalog; the placement rule quoted is Lanfry's rule for Ghadames Berber, which the authors tentatively transfer to Zenaga, so the specific initial/second-syllable alternation is not an independent Zenaga observation.
